title: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls
description: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-r
body: Embattled German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to stay on despite exit polls in two local elections suggesting damaging defeats for his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. In the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the party was projected to only just scrape into parliament, while the AfD was on track to win the most votes. Merz called the result "a disaster" for his party.In Berlin, the ruling CDU was also expected to be beaten by Die Linke (The Left).Merz is under mounting pressure, with poor approval ratings and rumours he could even be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap.Votes took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt.Echoing comments he made after that defeat, Merz told reporters on Sunday that he would forge ahead with his coalition government's plans to push through a package of economic, tax and welfare reforms."The reforms have to come," he insisted. "I am taking on this responsibility, because I want to move our country forward"."I would even go so far as to say that these reforms are the antidote to the authoritarian poison that, with the fascination of authoritarianism, is penetrating ever deeper into our society," Merz added.As the projected results came up on the screen at the CDU's election night gathering in Berlin, there were no cheers or celebration.This is a party that knows it's in trouble.Friedrich Merz is going on the offensive, quickly declaring he is going nowhere.He has long coveted the top job in German politics and likely won't give it up easily.Polls for both states closed at 18:00 local time (17:00 BST), with a final result expected in the coming hours.According to public broadcaster ZDF, the AfD was projected to take 38% of the vote share in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It was followed in second place by the centre-left SPD, on 36%.However, the AfD is unlikely to govern in the state as other parties refuse to work with it. For Berlin, the broadcaster put the CDU on 20% of the vote share when polls closed, behind Die Linke on nearly 26%.Prior to Sunday's elections, there had been intense speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced unless his party's political fortunes improved.Earlier this week, the leaders of eight German states backed Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months.While his backers have argued that many of the problems the nation faces are inherited, Merz himself is deeply unpopular.The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.

schema.headline: German state elections: Chancellor Friedrich Merz vows to stay on despite 'disaster' in polls

title: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
description: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.M
body: Ukraine has fired its largest drone attack on the Moscow region, the mayor has said, hitting the city's main oil refinery and a residential building.Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called "the most massive" attack. The region's governor said at least two people were killed and 20 injured.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region with drones and missiles, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".Ukrainian officials meanwhile said nine people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Andrei Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Governor Andrei Vorobyev added.Videos verified by the BBC on social media show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse.Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and the oil refinery - where Ukrainian military officials said three key units had been damaged.The site supplies more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, according to the defence ministry in Kyiv, and some of its petrol, diesel and aviation fuel go to Russia's military.Ukraine's defence minister said attacking such facilities "directly undermines the enemy's ability to continue its war of aggression and supply its military formations".Sobyanin said the major attack was "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election, which was in its third day on Sunday. The vote is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and has been dismissed by critics as neither free, fair nor transparent.Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Saturday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.Russia also struck a monastery in the Kherson region with a drone on Saturday, Zelensky said, killing one member of the clergy and injuring four others.Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

schema.headline: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says

title: Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader
description: A Liberal Democrat council leader has said the party is "sleepwalking into irrelevance" and questioned whether Sir Ed Davey was the right leader.Julia
body: A Liberal Democrat council leader has said the party is "sleepwalking into irrelevance" and questioned whether Sir Ed Davey was the right leader.Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon County Council, told the BBC the party was "lacking ambition" and "not saying the things that people can relate to".Asked whether Sir Ed was the right leader for the party, Brazil said "I wish he was" but "all the evidence is no".A Lib Dem spokesperson said the party was in "an incredibly strong position" under Sir Ed's leadership because he was focused on the "issues that really matter" such as the cost of living and the health service.  "Under Ed's leadership we had our best result for a century, and achieved a record breaking streak of remarkable local election results," they added."We are the most united party in Westminster and with Ed as leader we will stop Reform and the Conservatives and change our country after a decade of failing governments."Sir Ed led the party to record 72 MPs in the 2024 general election, but it has slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK.Brazil told the BBC the Lib Dems had "allowed other parties to go steaming past us," adding that "something has to change within the party if we're going to move to the next level and it's not happening at the moment".He added: "I think there is a fantastic opportunity now for us to be right in the middle of politics and we don't seem to be. We seem to be peripheral."We're lacking ambition, we're lacking courage of our convictions. We're not saying the things that people can relate to."He said the party was asking people to "vote for us because we're not somebody else".Brazil became the leader of Devon County Council in May last year after the Lib Dems overtook the Tories to become the largest party, but without overall control.His comments are echoed privately by some Lib Dem MPs, as they gather for their annual conference in Brighton.In an essay, written ahead of the conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".Sir Ed, who was elected leader in 2020, told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg he shared the "frustration" of some of his MPs that they could not bring about "real change," blaming the UK's political system.But he insisted the party was gaining ground in council elections."It's the most successful period that we've had," he said.  "But outside elections, in terms of changing the law, which is what my MPs rightly want to do, and they're a very talented bunch, and they've actually had more success than all the other smaller parties, but they want to have more."Sir Ed was asked directly about Brazil's complaints during a conference Q&A session on Sunday. "I have know Julian for many years and he is good councillor," he said."In Devon the party doing better than it has for decades - six MPs and local councils all across the area and in parts of Devon we are showing how to beat Reform."I'm really proud of what we have been doing in Devon."Sir Ed got a vote of confidence from former coalition cabinet colleague Sir Vince Cable, who told a fringe meeting that he was the most successful leader in the party's history and "you can't argue with success".Speaking at another fringe meeting, pollster Luke Tryl said the Lib Dems were not cutting through nationally and needed a more compelling message.The executive director of More in Common said it was possible the party could take more seats in traditional Tory heartlands at the next election, potentially putting Sir Ed in a position to be deputy prime minister in a Labour-led government.But the risk for the party, he added, was the Tories saying "if you vote Lib Dem you will get Labour".

schema.headline: Lib Dems sleepwalking to irrelevance under Davey, says council leader

title: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth
description: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and
body: Kelsey Parker, the widow of The Wanted singer Tom Parker, has welcomed a baby after last year announcing a "devastating" stillbirth.The podcaster and author, 35, had two children with British boy band star Tom Parker before he died in 2022, aged 33, after being diagnosed with terminal brain cancer.She is now in a relationship with Will Lindsay and last June revealed the "earth-shattering news" that they had lost their baby Phoenix.On Sunday, a post on her Instagram account showed a photo of a newborn baby's arm next to a pink sign with the word River. "Welcome to the world, River. Our little bit of hope," the caption said.Celebrities including The Saturdays singer Rochelle Humes, TV presenter Susanna Reid and reality TV star Holly Hagan-Blyth have congratulated Kelsey Parker on social media."Congratulations angel," Rochelle Humes wrote. "Oh my goodness – this is so wonderful – welcome River," Susanna Reid said.Hagan-Blyth commented "I am SO happy for you xxxx".Kelsey Parker's Instagram bio says "turning life's hardest moments into hope".Last year she posted a poem online after the loss of her stillborn baby.It was called Born Sleeping, Forever Loved, and began "the world grew quiet as you arrived, So loved, so longed for, yet not alive. Our precious boy, our angel light, Born with wings, took silent flight".

schema.headline: Kelsey Parker welcomes baby after 'devastating' stillbirth

title: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth
description: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe
body: Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too. And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters."We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, an… autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son". Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent"."And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work."I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says."I try to put all that in there… and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy."This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.There are new issues to concern ourselves with in mid-life and, as you'd expect, Horgan doesn't shy away from embarrassing situations or mildly unhealthy preoccupations.Her protagonist - who is 50 - has a slight obsession with sagging skin, which will no doubt strike a chord with many."It's really weird watching yourself age on screen because that's not fun," she reveals.Horgan says she wanted to offer "an honest depiction of someone having a complicated relationship with ageing". She adds that she herself has now formed "a better relationship" with getting older."I think it's OK to age any way you want to age. And we're insecure about it for a reason. And that's because it's shoved down our necks that we need to look a certain way, especially within the entertainment industry and in magazines. And women who age really well are celebrated just for that. And that is annoying."When it comes to sex, she says "you just have different insecurities" when you're a bit older."You think about angles, you think about the shapes you make and how to be sexy as an older woman. And, you, know, lighting comes into it! But I also have friends who are incredibly free with their bodies and feel like this is a whole new era and they're embracing it."I know that I will get there," she continues. "But I wanted to show a middle-aged woman having a complicated relationship with her body but still putting herself out there because... she wants to find someone to grow old with."Sherwood star Sharlene Whyte, who plays Horgan's boss and best friend Sam, says we need to see older women's stories on screen."We should see more of it - women who are later on in age, who have been privileged to get here later on, who are still killing it and are still beautiful and sexy and funny," she says."But I think women in their 50s are more visible (now)... and there's more (acting) work for women in later life."Despite the two lead characters being 50-something women, Whyte describes Youth as "an inter-generational watch".That's probably due to a prominent Gen Z storyline involving Alex's son, Ruari, played by 19-year-old Aran Murphy (Cillian Murphy's son. And yes, as you might expect, he's very good).Ruari has a difficult relationship with his feckless father - Alex's ex-husband (Owen McDonnell) - and in one poignant scene, describes how confusing it is to find your way as a young man in today's world."Having good people around you is so important, and it's not always easy to have that," Murphy muses."So, for someone like Ruari, when you don't have the foundation of friends and stuff, you look to the (wrong) kinds of people... and oftentimes, you'll be left out on your ass with the wrong answers."What does he hope young people who might catch the show will take away from it?"You don't have to have it all in place at 18, everyone is still kind of just pretending they know what they're doing."I suggest that we don't always know what we're doing in later life either.He laughs. "Exactly. Everyone's still figuring it out."Youth will debut on 21 September in the UK & Ireland on HBO Max.

schema.headline: Sex and dating in midlife - Sharon Horgan on her new comedy Youth

title: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found
description: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year
body: Image source, Police handoutImage caption, Joanne Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020ByCurtis LancasterSouth of EnglandA 56-year-old man has been rearrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and further arrested on suspicion of murder after human remains were identified as a missing mother-of-three.Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham, London, on 12 August after bones were found in shrubland damaged by a fire a week earlier.The man, from Southampton, first arrested in 2020, has been released on conditional bail. Another man, also 56 and from Southampton, was released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The human remains were found at Padstow Walk in Feltham, south-west LondonSheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force said led to more than 4,000 lines of inquiry, more than 300 statements taken and searches of more than 10 addresses and numerous water vessels. Sheen was reported missing by her family in February 2020, two months after she was last seen.An investigation led to a number of arrests on suspicion of conspiracy to murder in 2020, but no-one was charged and the case remained unsolved.Officers previously said she had no fixed address and did not own a vehicle or hold a bank account.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The area damaged by the fire was cordoned off after the remains were found by a member of the publicLondon Fire Brigade attended a fire at Bedfont Pits on 5 August that damaged about two hectares of shrubland.The Metropolitan Police said human remains were found by a member of the public at the site near Bedfont Lakes Country Park a week later. Detectives in London handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

schema.headline: Southampton man rearrested after missing mum's remains found

title: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana
description: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duches
body: Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face."If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied."And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example."I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan. He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997. In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness". His comments about the Sussexes come just weeks after the pair returned to the UK.They have long been critical of their treatment by the British press as well as the support they received from the Royal Family prior to their decision to leave the UK.Speaking in the couple's 2021 interview with Oprah Winfrey, Prince Harry accused the tabloid media of having created a "toxic environment" of "control and fear".Meghan, meanwhile, said in the couple's 2022 Netflix series that "no matter how hard I tried, no matter how good I was, no matter what I did, they [the media] were still going to find a way to destroy me".In July this year, Prince Harry and six others including Liz Hurley and Sir Elton John lost a privacy case against the publisher of the Daily Mail, and may face a legal bill of up to £34.5m.In separate, earlier legal battles, the Duke of Sussex beat the Mirror Group in court, and the News Group out of court, forcing a settlement, damages, payout and apology.Earl Spencer's interview with the BBC was his first since the Palace issued a strongly worded response to his claims about King Charles.That statement said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Earl Spencer, in comments first reported on Friday, reacted to it by saying: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"He added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life."I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".In his response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Earl Spencer accused the King of psychological manipulation over the palace's statement."It is not every day you wake up to find you've been gaslit by the King," he said. "It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I'd lied without the King being able to deny what I'd said".Journalist Richard Kay, who had been close friends with Diana, also wrote in the newspaper on Sunday that in the week between her death and funeral, Earl Spencer had told him of a "furious row" with Charles."It was 'about the boys', but he was reluctant to go further," said Kay, adding that Earl Spencer said the then prince had been "utterly pathetic".However, speaking to BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House on Sunday, Dame Julia Cleverdon, a trusted aide and friend of the King, said the claims about his response to Diana's death did not reflect "the language or the behaviours of a man I've known for 40 years".Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family.In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner".Dame Julia said: "To say that the Prince of Wales was elated and somehow took any pleasure... he was as if a 10-tonne truck had fallen on him.Her own husband had died a fortnight before Diana and she said Charles "could not have been more supportive, loving, concerned about the children and interested".

schema.headline: Earl Spencer tells BBC Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana

title: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?
description: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrive
body: Image caption, Laura Kuenssberg met Earl Spencer at Althorp, the ancestral home on the grounds of which Diana is buriedByPolitical editorWhen I arrived at Althorp on Thursday to speak to Charles, Earl Spencer, only a handful of people were in evidence in the vast stately home, where Princess Diana had once tapdanced in the hall and rollerskated in the cavernous library.It was only hours after Buckingham Palace had sent out its blistering statement in response to the explosive claims made in a new book by Earl Spencer. From the particularly English peace of this grand countryside setting, Diana's brother had provoked a storm.That Palace statement, questioning Earl Spencer's account of the days after his sister's death, was a total contrast to its normal "never explain, never complain" mantra. But it meant that as we sat down, with oil paintings of Earl Spencer's aristocratic ancestors staring down at our TV lights, the interview was not just about his recollections of his sister. It had become about whether the earl, or the King himself, was telling the truth. As we asked Earl Spencer: which Charles are we meant to believe?Figure caption, 'There was a lightness in his tone', says Earl Spencer about Charles' reaction to Diana's deathThat's why it was so important to test Earl Spencer's claims. Was he really sure that the then-Prince Charles had sounded "giddy" after his former wife had died on that terrible night in 1997? Both men, after all, were in a moment of profound shock.Did the earl, a historian and former journalist himself, have evidence of another of his memories, that Charles had "hissed" at him that the world would "forget her soon enough"? Why does he, the uncle of William and Harry, think the world needs to hear his version of events from all those years ago?Earl Spencer was resolute; strong in his conviction that his version of events needed to be told as a matter of record. And he recounted his memories of his conversations with the King in meticulous detail, noting carefully in our discussion that the Palace had not explicitly denied his claims, instead choosing to question his judgement.There is deep unhappiness and frustration in Buckingham Palace at what Earl Spencer has put into the public domain. Their strongly worded statement tells you everything you need to know about how upset they are. "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.Bear in mind that the two Charleses have had a difficult relationship for decades. Even before either of them was born, the Spencers and the Windsors, two aristocratic families, had years of splits and spats. In the past 48 hours, allies on either side have lined up to back the two different accounts, with acolytes of the King suggesting he would never have said such things. Others emerged to back Spencer.There is no way of being completely sure what exactly happened. There hasn't been an explicit denial, but the Palace has objected in very strong terms to how Earl Spencer has presented the past. But speaking to Diana's brother for about half an hour, I felt he seemed entirely sure in his own mind. His book is carefully constructed to give his account, as well as pay tribute to his sister's life as the 30th anniversary of her death approaches.Princess Diana: My Sister's StoryWatch the full interview with Laura Kuenssberg.After we had spoken, we walked down to the lake on the estate where, on a wooded island, Diana was laid to rest. It's a place where, Earl Spencer told me, she could be safe from intrusion, and is marked as a burial place with a huge stone urn.We passed the little green rowing boat he uses to go to the island to visit her, and walked to what he calls The Temple. It's an 18th Century building that now bears her name and includes a quote from her and another from his famous eulogy to her. It's a line he now says was specifically intended to be a riposte to the other Charles' suggestion that she would quickly be forgotten: Diana "will never be extinguished from our minds".Earl Spencer told me he was not being "vengeful" and that he was not trying to damage the monarchy - even saying there was more he knew about the King that he could relate but had chosen not to. But by speaking out so boldly, publishing his book, serialising it in the papers, and speaking to us, the earl was not just paying a moving tribute to his sister, but stirring up the long-running contest for control of Diana's memory.Figure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaIn the closing moments of our interview, Earl Spencer revealed himself not to be a public figure trying to settle old scores or correct myths about his incredibly famous sister. When I asked how much he missed her, he welled up, and nearly three decades on, the tears still came. He said he missed her every day. "The thing with sibling loss? You never get over it," he said.Charles Spencer was a young man when his sister died at 36 in the most awful circumstances. He joked about crying as a 62-year-old man at the end of a TV interview in which he'd discussed the monarchy and also made claims about the King that he was well aware would stir up controversy around the world. In the normally hidden world of Althorp, the grief of a brother was still plainly on display – what happened to Princess Diana is not all in the past.

schema.headline: Laura Kuenssberg: I asked Earl Spencer who we should believe, him or the King?

title: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty
description: Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cuttin
body: Sir Ed Davey is calling on the government to immediately cut fuel duty by 10p a litre until Christmas as part of a package of policies aimed at cutting the cost of living.The Liberal Democrat leader is also urging the government to scrap a permanent increase in fuel duty which is set to take effect in January.Fuel duty was frozen under the Conservatives in March 2022 and Sir Keir Starmer's government continued the freeze, deciding in May to push back a planned 3p increase in September until the end of this year.The Lib Dems claim cutting 10p from fuel duty now would mean fuel would drop by 12p per litre at the pump.Sir Ed claimed drivers should be supported and a temporary three-month fuel duty cut would pay for itself by stimulating the economy."Petrol and diesel prices are higher than they've been for a long time because of Trump's mad war with Iran, and people need help now," he said. The policy would cost about £2bn, he said, adding: "It's a three-month package, a temporary package, but if you look at the extra money the government will get through the energy profits levy, from gas taxes, from VAT and fuel duty, it's self-funding."In a speech to his party's conference on Tuesday, Sir Ed will make further calls to cut the bus fare cap from £3 to £1, and reduce rail fares by 10%.He will also call for VAT to be dropped from public charging points for electric vehicles and a review of network costs the Lib Dems have labelled unfair. Chancellor John Healey is under pressure to raise taxes or cut spending at his Budget next month, amid soaring government borrowing costs.Asked about Sir Ed's call for a fuel duty cut, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson told Laura Kuenssberg: "I'm sure John Healey will be open to any and all suggestions ahead of the budget but actually this is an area where the Labour government has taken action on fuel duty already."Whilst I recognise what the Lib Dems have to say on this topic, this is the element of politics about it - they've got their conference, they're making their pitch, good luck to them."Sir Ed also ruled out scrapping the state pension triple lock after party grandee and former business secretary Sir Vince Cable said at a fringe event it was unsustainable and should be "phased out".Speaking at Q&A on the conference stage, Sir Ed said the policy had been introduced by the Lib Dems during the Conservative coalition to address inequalities and there was still work to do to tackle pensioner poverty."It has not finished the job," he told party members, who were split in a show of hands about whether the triple lock should be scrapped if the Lib Dems win power.The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but critics say it is unaffordable and unfair to younger people.

schema.headline: Ed Davey calls for immediate 10p cut to fuel duty

title: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity
description: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisatio
body: As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation."It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says."In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.But despite having their support while he's relatively independent, Norman says he worries about the prospect of facing discrimination if he needs more formal care as he ages."Hopefully I will maintain and look after myself the best I can, but I've heard horror stories of gay people in nursing homes being treated terribly," he says."I think nurses, doctors, carers should all be trained on how to look after LGBT people."It's the reason behind schemes like Manchester's Kindred House, which are not unusual in other parts of the world.There are similar projects in Spain, Sweden, Germany, the US and Canada, but in the UK they are few and far between.In 2021, the UK's first LGBTQ+ retirement home, Tonic, opened in London with 19 apartments for private rental or shared ownership.The scheme attracted so much attention, later this year it is set to feature in a Netflix documentary telling the story of one of its first residents, Chek Min-Ong.After 43 years together, Min, 77, and his late partner Tim, had discussed their plans for a future where one of them would live alone, as Tim's health deteriorated.While schemes like Kindred House and Tonic are welcomed by Mindy, Norman and Min, the Spotlight on Ageing report warns that, because the older LGBTQ+ population is growing, the demand for specialist services is expected to outstrip supply.Between 2019 and 2024, the number of over-50s identifying as lesbian, gay or bisexual in the UK increased by around a third - from roughly 340,000 to almost 460,000.There was a 4% rise in the number of heterosexual people aged 50 and above in the same period.These numbers are projected to continue to increase as the relatively larger younger generations of people identifying as LGBTQ+ age.Porter warns that without more schemes like Kindred House, and more training and awareness for those in other care settings, the ageing population may struggle to get proper support.For Mindy, who is part of a steering group advising on the plans, knowing there may be more options available in the future is reassuring."It's important that you can go, that you think, 'You know what, I could live there because I know the staffing, the ethics, the rules, everything about the place has been put together from an LGBTQ+ focus,'" she says."That's what we've been doing and it's something I'm really proud of being a part of."

schema.headline: Why growing older LGBTQ+ community in Britain fears losing identity

title: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married
description: The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My TeacherWatch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monda
body: The full story with be available in subsequent episodes of World of Secrets Catching My TeacherWatch the full investigation on iPlayer from 0001 Monday 21 September. If you are outside the UK, you will be able watch on YouTubeYusron began investigating Abah a year previously, sparked by a revelation one night by his former classmate Ziadatur Rahmah. They had both been star pupils at Lombok's Abu Barokat school. Now they were at university - Yusron in the capital Jakarta, and Ziadatur in Cairo, Egypt - and had begun reminiscing over the phone about their school days.One night Ziadatur, known to her friends as Zia, told Yusron that Abah had sexually assaulted her when she was 16.She had needed to go to the toilet during class and Abah had intercepted her in the school gardens and asked her to accompany him to his house which was on the premises. Once inside, he had told her he loved her, she told Yusron."He pulled me down so I was sitting on his lap… Then he started kissing me… He was stroking and touching my body," she later told the BBC World Service, too, explaining that he told her to do the same to him.Luckily, she said, one of his children began banging on the locked front door. Abah signalled to her to leave and she bolted out the back. But the effect was devastating."I felt very dirty, ruined, and I was lost."Yusron, when he heard Zia's account, was unsure what to do. Their school had inculcated them with the motto: "Sami'na wa ata'na" ["We hear, and we obey"].But he also could not stop thinking about it.So he suggested that he and Zia, together with her school friends Wanda Hamidah and Mahima Eka, gather corroborating evidence to support her testimony.And slowly, as they spoke to their old classmates, other recollections emerged - the friends sharing their findings with each other on WhatsApp.The most significant was from a friend of Wanda's. She recalled seeing a younger girl crying in the school bathroom during their final year, late at night. And that Abah had come looking for her, red-faced and panting.This girl, Sukma Rohana, was still at the school. She told the BBC about her ordeal.When Sukma was 17, Abah had asked her to join him for new year's prayers, she told us. When she entered Abah's house, he had covered her mouth and told her to lie down, she said, before he stripped below the waist."He kept talking, saying he couldn't control himself any more," Sukma said."He was feeling me up through my knickers… He tried to rape me."And then, she said, she had found the strength to kick him hard in the stomach and took the opportunity to flee.As she ran, she said she had looked back to see his torch seeking her out.As evidence like this emerged, Yusron would co-ordinate it - following up with calls to the students making the allegations, and keeping painstaking notes.He typed up a seven-page document outlining the alleged abuse of Sukma, Zia and four other former students.Wanda organised a meeting with representatives from the Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI) - the powerful organisation that ran their school and hundreds of others, and which was also funding some of the students' studies in Cairo.The meeting went well, the friends told us - the NWDI representatives had said they would help them take the case to the police.But three weeks later, when Yusron received that ominous text from his sister - calling back to find Abah on the end of the phone in Yusron's family home - it became clear the NWDI had passed on Yusron's written documents to him."If this is leaked to the media… I'll be destroyed," Abah can be heard saying on Yusron's recording of him.He pleads with Yusron to lie for him, giving him a series of cover stories he can use to retract his evidence document.He then called Zia and exerted similar pressure. Like Yusron, she recorded the call. In it, Abah admits he abused her but pleads with her to stay silent.Sukma, for her part, told us she was called to Abah's house to discover two police officers and an NWDI lawyer waiting for her. They forced her to sign a document saying all her allegations were lies, she said. Her account is backed up by a secret recording she later made as she challenged Abah's wife, Hurmiati.Hurmiati can be heard telling her to respect their "agreement" that nothing happened, adding: "Do you want this to haunt you for the rest of your life? Do you want it to damage the chances of you getting married?"This pressure even extended to Abah asking Yusron's parents to fly to Jakarta to look for him at university. They didn't find him - he was hiding in a hotel - but the ordeal was too much for Yusron's mother. She told her son the stress was killing her.So Yusron reluctantly stopped his investigation.Meanwhile he and Zia were slowly getting closer. The friendship had become a long-distance relationship, and they were regularly speaking on the phone."And I could see she was really struggling… She'd say things like: 'Why do I keep thinking about what [Abah] did?'."Yusron was torn between helping the girl he was falling in love with, and the promise he had made to his mother.And then, eight months later, Yusron heard about a group raising awareness about sexual abuse in Islamic schools. It had been set up by a young woman called Ayu Masruroh, who had helped her friend get justice after she had been sexually assaulted at another school, by a teacher called Moch Subchi Azal Tsani.Ayu was now actively posting on social media about the need to speak out.It inspired Zia to post a call-out on Instagram, asking any Indonesian student who had experienced abuse to get in touch.And she was to discover that, despite Abah's remonstrations, and promises to change, he had apparently offended again. Someone who went to Zia's school got in touch to say she too had been sexually exploited by Abah. The alleged abuse had taken place almost a year after his pledges to Zia and Yusron."It made me realise [Abah] hadn't really changed at all… all the things he said about stopping… It was all just lies," said Zia.If you are in the UK, and have been affected by issues of sexual abuse or violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineYusron's parents finally agreed he should help Zia and Sukma to continue their quest for justice.But this time, the friends decided to do things differently. They contacted Ayu, and she was clear: get a lawyer. She introduced them to someone experienced in representing sexual abuse survivors. He advised that Sukma's case was the strongest to ensure a prosecution.We contacted Abah and Hurmiati about the allegations against them - they did not respond.NWDI said it was still investigating the allegations internally and denied ever trying to cover up sexual abuse claims.It said it had "a duty to safeguard the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals".Sukma filed her claim against Abah to the police in February last year. She is still waiting for them to take action and Abah is still in post."I don't want what happened to me, to happen to any other students. I want justice," she told the BBC.The investigation has, however, brought Zia and Yusron ever closer. Last February, after three years of messaging and speaking, Yusron decided to move to Cairo to be with her."I was exhausted. Jakarta had been intense, because I was dealing with the police case the whole time. So when I saw Zia… it was like medicine," he told the BBC.Zia said she was so happy she "started talking non-stop."That's when I knew he was serious. He had come all the way to Egypt for me. I trust him. That's why I'm with him."It is a trust built, in part, on their shared pursuit of justice. Last month the couple got married.Their lawyer, Joko Jumadi, says he has been struck by the students' courage and precision.The recordings they secretly collected, he told us, capture the pressure to stay silent in real time and are exceptionally valuable. "Several victims are mentioned - acknowledged by the individual himself. These are key pieces of evidence," he said.Joko and his team have handled 20 sexual abuse cases involving Islamic boarding schools in his local West Nusa Tenggara province over the past three years, and he believes this is "just the tip of the iceberg".

schema.headline: Our head teacher was an abuser. We joined forces to get justice - now we're married

title: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroinByScotland editorUpdated 20 September 2026 09:
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nitazenes are a class of synthetic opioids often sold as heroinByScotland editorUpdated 20 September 2026 09:04 BSTEfforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.  In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe."The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.Image caption, Forensic scientist Lorna Nisbet says the illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more dangerousUnlike heroin or cocaine, which are derived from cultivated plants, many of the new substances are manufactured in clandestine laboratories. They include synthetic opioids such as nitazenes and orphines, some of which are hundreds of times more potent than heroin.Police say organised crime groups are increasingly mixing the substances with existing drugs to maximise their profits."I think it's shameful behaviour that we're seeing from these organised crime groups," Supt Niven Bull, of Police Scotland, said."They are profiting from people's misery."On average, a new psychoactive substance emerged every week in 2025, according to the European Union Drugs Agency (EUDA)., external The agency says tighter controls imposed by China and the Taliban's ban on poppy cultivation in Afghanistan have pushed production closer to consumer markets.That includes Scotland, where police have raided two suspected nitazene factories in the past 14 months, making five arrests in total.In July 2025, officers discovered an alleged illicit drugs laboratory in Patna, Ayrshire, leading to the arrest of three people.Deputy Chief Constable Jane Connors later described it as the UK's first suspected nitazene laboratory.BBC News can also reveal that two men, aged 43 and 56, were arrested in February this year after police searched a unit in Loanhead, Midlothian, as part of an investigation into another suspected synthetic opioid lab.In 2024, nitazenes were implicated in 76 drug-related deaths in Scotland, according to official figures, external, more than three times the number of the previous year."These drugs are extremely dangerous, and it's pretty rapid for us to be able to keep up as scientists," says Dr Nisbet, whose laboratory is soon set to take on an expanded role as Scotland's national drug testing facility.The changing nature of the supply also creates challenges for lawmakers who are in a race to identify and ban dangerous new substances before they can spread legally and cause havoc."New and harmful substances continue to be created to circumvent legal controls,"  EUDA points out.While control of illicit drugs is reserved to Westminster under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, responsibility for public health, policing and prosecutions is devolved to the Scottish government and its agencies.Image caption, Gareth Balmer says this is a frightening new landscapeOn the front line of the battle to save lives, charity workers say they are seeing the devastating impact of the new synthetic opioids first-hand.In the woods at Glenbarr on the Kintyre peninsula, staff from the drug, alcohol and mental health charity With You are trying to treat trauma in a group designed to help former drug and alcohol users reconnect with nature.Gareth Balmer, the charity's national harm reduction lead, says nitazenes and other synthetic opioids are now appearing across the drug supply, from benzodiazepine (street Valium) pills and cannabinoids, known as spice, to cocaine and heroin."This is a frightening new landscape," he said. "I don't think drugs have ever been as risky or as dangerous as they are now."The result is that some users are experiencing unexpected and sometimes catastrophic overdoses."Some of these substances are so potent that a grain would be enough to take somebody over," Balmer warned, adding that access to naloxone, which can reverse the effects of an opioid overdose, is now more important than ever.Bull said Police Scotland was taking a twin-track approach, promising to "relentlessly pursue" dealers while also recognising that many drug users need help.In 2025, officers seized about £80m worth of street drugs. So far this year that figure has already reached £78m."Hundreds of individuals have been arrested, and many people are serving custodial sentences," Bull said.But he added that the force also wanted to help users "to make better life choices"."If we come across people who are suffering from addiction, who are in a low point in their life, then we will look to help support them and we'll look to refer them to the relevant agency," he said.Image caption, Prof Niamh Nic Daeid says her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communitiesProf Niamh Nic Daeid, director of Dundee University's Leverhulme laboratory, said its expanded role as a national drug testing and research centre would make a difference too.On one hand, she said, her team will be able to provide near real-time information to drug-using communities, allowing them to make safer and more informed choices. On the other, the research will help to inform government policy."Drugs are changing all the time," she said. "Part of the establishment of this facility is to have a research capability that will enable us to try to keep up."If we don't know what substances are present in the samples, how can we provide the right advice?"Image caption, Vicky Gamble is worried about the emerging threat of new substancesBack in Kintyre, Vicky Gamble, whose own struggles with alcohol, drugs and crime have seen her in and out of prison, is enjoying the tranquillity of the forest.She is personally hopeful of a better future but she is worried about the emerging threat of new substances and the potential effect on friends and family."It seems that there's a lot of stuff that all the young ones seem to be taking now and I don't even think they know what it is," she told me.For Gareth Balmer of With You, that uncertainty is part of the danger.He says: "It's a terrible thing to say, but with heroin it was better the devil you knew."

schema.headline: The deadly new drugs making Scotland's fight against addiction even harder

title: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King
description: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Updated 3 hours agoEarl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its cr
body: ByAndré Rhoden-Paul Updated 3 hours agoEarl Spencer has told the BBC writing his book about sister Princess Diana, which has made headlines for its criticism of King Charles, was his "duty...as an eyewitness to history".In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the memoir's release on Tuesday, Earl Spencer said he wanted "to put things down once and for all that were true".Among claims made in Swan Song about the King, who was then the Prince of Wales, was that he said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.In a strongly worded response, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".Here are the key moments from Earl Spencer's interview, which include his first account of how he was told about Diana's death and criticism of press coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Earl initially told Diana's crash was 'not too serious'Earl Spencer was in South Africa when Princess Diana died in a Paris car crash in the early hours of 31 August 1997, along with close friend Dodi Fayed and the driver of the car.He told the BBC he got a call in the middle of the night from his sister Lady Jane Fellowes, who said Princess Diana had been in a crash but "it's not too serious". But then he "kept getting more and more distressing calls" from his sister. "And then my sister Jane said, 'I'm afraid she's died.' It started... as a little prang, and then it became a broken leg, perhaps a head injury, and then death."Charles had 'giddy tone' after Diana's deathFigure caption, Earl Spencer describes 'giddy tone' in Charles' voice during call after Diana's deathDescribing the hours after her death, Earl Spencer said he took a call at his home in Cape Town from Prince Charles, who told him how he broke the news to Princes William and Harry at Balmoral Castle. "I felt there was a sort of giddy tone," he told the BBC. "I'd had a lot of calls that day from people who cared, who were stunned... and I just felt there was a lightness in his tone about Diana's death that really jarred with me."In his book, Earl Spencer compares his tone to like a "lottery winner" and says he suspects the prince's reaction was based on how this event would free him to marry the woman he loved, his future wife Queen Camilla. When asked by Kuenssberg if he could be sure that is what Prince Charles was thinking, Earl Spencer said: "I cannot be sure, I'm saying that's what I assume from the tone is a possibility." Image caption, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story. The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg is available on BBC iPlayer and will be broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday Earl Spencer told the BBC he had been discussing funeral arrangements with a palace official, who said it had been agreed Princes William and Harry should walk behind their mother's coffin. Unhappy, he said he told the official it is not what his sister would have wanted, before the conversation came to an end. Soon after, the earl says he took a call from Prince Charles, who asked him about his opposition to it. "I said, 'Well, of course not, sir, she wouldn't want it'. And then he said, 'Well, I walked behind Lord Mountbatten's coffin.' And I said, 'Yes, but you were 30 and he wasn't your mother'."He then claims Charles went "ballistic... and ranted for a while" about the Spencer's sense of duty not being adequate enough before "he said 'We'll forget her [Diana] soon enough'.""I really was so stunned and after a stunned silence I said 'I can not believe you just said that' and I hung up on him", the earl told Kuenssberg during his sit down interview at his Althorp estate. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Princes William and Harry walked in the procession behind their mother's coffinResponding to the Palace's statement pushing back on the story, Earl Spencer said: "I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said. "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage in my life. "I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said. And I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. "I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."The earl said he told "close friends and family" about the "monstrous" comment. When asked if people should believe him or the King, he said: "Well, I'm telling the truth... what else would have made me hang up on the King that day?"On what Princes William and Harry might think of the comments being brought up nearly 30 years later, he added the words "will not be a surprise" to the brothers.He also said his renowned funeral eulogy, in which he said his sister's qualities would never be "extinguished from our minds", was a "direct rebuttal" of the prince's comments. 'I know lots of things about the King' not in the bookTalking about his motivations for writing the book, Earl Spencer, aged 62, said it was his "duty... as an eyewitness to history" and as someone in the "final season of my life" with his parents dying in their sixties."I'm aware of mortality and I wanted to just put things down once and for all that were true," the historian and journalist explained."This is not a threat, it's a fact, I know lots of things about the King which I chose not to include in the book because they were not relevant."When put to him that the  statement sounded like a threat when it involved potentially damaging information, he said: "No, not at all a threat, it's just the reality."Kuenssberg questioned why he included an account of a conversation in which his sister told him Prince Charles was in love with his valet - a claim Earl Spencer said was improbable - and asked if he was motivated in including some of these allegations to create interest to sell the book. "It's in the context of a conversation where Diana is telling me that her marriage is over," the earl replied."It's a brother's tribute, a loving tribute to a sister.  And I think she deserves honesty so that's what I've delivered."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Earl Spencer said he was concerned about security for Duke and Duchess of SussexEarl Spencer worries about Harry's lack of police protectionWhen asked about how he thinks Prince Harry has been treated by the Royal Family, Earl Spencer told the BBC he is reluctant to discuss it, but he said he was concerned about his security. "I would say that I personally worry about the fifth-in-line to the throne who's served in the military not having any police protection," he said. "As an uncle who's seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, that I would veer towards protection."It is understood the committee that oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now they and their two children are full-time residents in the UK rather than visitors.When asked about how the press treated Princess Diana and now Prince Harry and Meghan, he said tabloid articles "could be really really unpleasant". "It would really be beholden on people to learn from Diana's example. I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life," Earl Spencer said. "[Diana] was really brought low by all that criticism. And yeah I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The earl said he hopes his nephews resolve their differences'I hope William and Harry resolve row' Earl Spencer said he did not take sides - as he perceives is the "perception in the media" - in the dispute between Princes William and Harry. "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them. And if either of them wanted anything then I'd be equally there for them," he said. "And I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure I hope."He said there are a "lot of reasons on both sides" why the brothers' relationship had "got to this stage". "I hope one day it's resolved, but I don't know all – I certainly don't know what's been done in the finer detail and so I would feel intrusive if I got more involved than to say of course a mother would want her two sons to be happy together and love each other," he said. Diana 'convinced she couldn't trust people' after Bashir interviewReflecting on the time before Princess Diana's death, Kuenssberg asked if the infamous BBC Panorama interview with journalist Martin Bashir in 1995 might have been linked indirectly to his sister finding herself in Paris in 1997. Shortly after the interview broadcast, in which Princess Diana admitted having an affair and said Prince Charles's affair with then-Camilla Parker Bowles made her feel worthless, the Queen wrote to Prince Charles and Princess Diana telling them to divorce.A 2021 inquiry found Bashir acted in a "deceitful" way  by mocking up fake bank statements - which falsely suggested individuals were being paid to keep Diana under surveillance - and showing them to Earl Spencer to gain access to the late princess.Earl Spencer said he did make "a connection" between the crash and the Panorama interview and said they conned both him and Diana."People said, 'Oh, she was paranoid'. She wasn't paranoid. She was convinced that she couldn't trust people because the evidence was there.  And, you know, I think that left her vulnerable that night."The BBC and Bashir apologised to King Charles, Earl Spencer and Princes William and Harry after the 2021 report was published.The BBC's then-director general, Tim Davie, said: "Although the report states that Diana, Princess of Wales, was keen on the idea of an interview with the BBC, it is clear that the process for securing the interview fell far short of what audiences have a right to expect. We are very sorry for this."Earl supports 'a modern monarchy'Earl Spencer, the ninth earl of an aristocratic family whose peerage dates back to the 18th Century and retains its vast estate, told the BBC he is "all for a monarchy, but I like a modern monarchy". Talking about the "jarring" protocol around the monarchy, he said: "You know, you mentioned the statement earlier, 'His Majesty says", I just don't think it's healthy for a human being to be seen in such archaic, servile terms."When Kuenssberg asked him if he supported this monarchy, following the damning book he has just written, he said: "I do."He added when challenged: "Well, I'm not dealing with King Charles as monarch in this book, this is all 30-odd years ago and what was said and done then."An emotional tribute to a sister he misses every dayFigure caption, Watch: 'You never get over it': Earl Spencer's emotional tribute to late sister DianaAs the interview came to an end, Earl Spencer was asked whether he would ever be able to get over his sister's death.Visibly emotional, he said he misses Diana "every day", adding "that's the thing with sibling loss, you never get over it."But his upcoming book, he said, is a way for him to have a final say on Diana's life before stepping off "into the sunset"."One of the reasons I called this Swan Song actually is because it's my sign off," he said."I have been Diana's brother, this is my final take on the situation… I'm not here to bang on about Diana, this is my final word, a celebration of her."

schema.headline: Key takeaways from BBC interview as Earl Spencer defends claims about King

title: Fulham v Man Utd player ratings: Matheus Cunha saves Man Utd with last minute equaliser
description: Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeu
body: Bernd Leno: On his toes to make an early save from Lisandro Martinez and scrambling when Matheus Cunha's effort looped on to a post. Denied Bryan Mbeumo with full-length save. 7Timothy Castagne: Booked for bringing Marcus Rashford down as Manchester United broke in the second half. 6David Affengruber: Excellent defence-splitting pass to release Josh King, but he couldn't finish. Exceptionally fortunate to escape after being outwitted by Cunha close to the goalline but stepped in to take the ball off Mbeumo as he looked to counter. 7Calvin Bassey: Not the easiest game positionally as Manchester United played without an orthodox centre-forward. Got forward to create Fulham's goal. 7Antonee Robinson: Pushed into advanced areas in the inside forward position, which caused the visitors a defensive issue. 7Sander Berge (Off, Larsson 76): Shot from the edge of the area turned away by Senne Lammens. 7Shea Charles: Midfield partnership with Berge was key in protecting the Fulham defence when the visitors had extended spells of possession around the home area. Passing let him down on occasion. 6Oscar Bobb (off Kevin, 70): Rolled an effort just wide of the post and probably should have done better. 6Josh King (off Andersen, 79): Always looking to get on the ball and threaten. Took a good save from Lammens to deny him at the far post and his shot across goal was going in without the visitors' keeper kicking it away. Blotted his copybook by getting booked for diving. 8Alex Iwobi (off Palacios, 70): Also tried to exploit the inside left channel when Fulham went forward. Low cross almost created a chance for Gonzalo Garcia and another deep one did for King. 7Gonzalo Garcia (off Muniz, 79): Half a stride away from having a tap-in from an Iwobi cross from the left. 6Subs:Palacios (on 70, Iwobi): Kept Fulham ticking over. 6Kevin (on 70, Bobb): Settled in well. 6Larsson (on 76, Berge): 6Muniz (on 79, Garcia): 6Andersen (on 79, King): 6Subs not used: Lecomte, Manuel Angel, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe.Senne Lammens: Key first-half saves to keep Manchester United level and came out bravely at Iwobi's feet to prevent another Fulham chance. Distribution could have been better and he didn't cover himself in glory with the Fulham goal. 6Diogo Dalot: Tidy spin and dash into space to create a chance for Rashford but had too much work to do defensively as he lacked cover far too often. 6Harry Maguire: Used his experience to draw a foul out of King as United tried to deal with Fulham pressure near their own goal. 7Lisandro Martinez: Well-struck half-volley drew an excellent save out of Leno. He did eventually find the net - at the wrong end. 5Luke Shaw (off Dorgu, 83): Returned from a three-match absence. Carrick's side are far more balanced when he is there. 7Youri Tielemans: Wasted an excellent opportunity when he got no power behind his effort as he ran on to Rashford's short pass. 5Kobbie Mainoo (off 79, Mount): Usual tidy game in possession without making the key passes. Never looks flustered. 7Bryan Mbeumo: A lot of strong runs but, like many Man Utd forwards, nowhere near his best. Tough ask, but did he give Dalot enough defensive support? 6Bruno Fernandes: Low shot against the post from Cunha cut-back but once more not at last season's levels. 6Marcus Rashford (off 76, Zirkzee): Tried to set up Tielemans with a short pass but the Belgian couldn't finish. An attempt of his own before the break was saved by Leno and another, better opportunity flew way over the bar. 6Matheus Cunha: Again started in the number nine role he doesn't seem suited to but created an excellent opportunity for Fernandes. Deflected shot hit the post and spun wide. Probably the visitors' most dangerous forward. 7Subs:Zirkzee (on 76, Rashford): 6Mount (on 79, Mainoo): 6Dorgu (on 83, Shaw): 7Subs not used: Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Yoro, Andrey Santos, Baleba, Lacey.

title: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US
description: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted
body: "Donald Trump is trying to claim he's got a success in Greenland, but actually, all he's got is almost a carbon copy of the agreement that's persisted since the 1950s," he said at a Q&A with members at party conference."So let Donald Trump try to pretend he's had a victory. The truth is, Europe, Nato, countries like Canada stood up to him and won."Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China.In the wake of the deal, Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week.The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen.The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted.Burnham has spoken with Trump at least twice since entering Downing Street and No 10 said he intends to use the UNGA to "drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home" including the cost of living and the war in Ukraine.

schema.headline: Burnham hails Greenland deal ahead of first Trump meeting in US
